before.model: I want to flag something about capacity before it becomes a problem. I'm currently running four projects, and two of them — Orsan and the migration — both need me most days. As a result I'm doing the reporting late in the evening, and last week I missed a deadline on the smaller one for the first time. It's not sustainable through to April. What I'd propose is handing the vendor reporting to Priya, who's asked for more responsibility anyway, and I'd keep the two big ones. That would put me back to something realistic. Could we look at that this week?
before.feedback: Notice what this does: it frames the issue as a risk to the work rather than a personal complaint, gives one hard piece of evidence (the missed deadline), and arrives with a solution that also helps someone else. Managers can act on this in one conversation.

after.brief: Different situation: a team member tells you they are overwhelmed. You are the manager.
after.prompt: Speak for 60 seconds: respond to them. Acknowledge, get specific, and agree a next step.
checklist: I acknowledged before problem-solving
I asked at least one question to get specifics
I did not immediately minimise it ('everyone's busy')
I agreed a concrete next step with a time
I used softening language rather than instructions
after.model: Thank you for telling me — that's not an easy thing to raise, and I'd much rather know now. Can I ask a couple of things so I understand the shape of it? Which of the four is taking the most time, and is it the volume or is something specific getting stuck? … Right. So if I'm hearing it correctly, it's mainly the reporting rather than the projects themselves. Let's do this: I'll look at whether that can move this week, and let's put twenty minutes in on Thursday to see if it's actually made a difference. And if it hasn't, we'll look at it again — I don't want this sitting unresolved for a month.
after.feedback: The key move is asking a diagnostic question before offering a solution. 'Is it the volume or is something getting stuck?' usually reveals that the real problem is narrower than 'everything', which makes it fixable.

before.brief: You are writing a business case for a sustainability change that costs money now and saves later. The budget committee will read it.
before.prompt: Select every argument that belongs in the written case. Wrong selections cost points.

options.text: The payback period is under three years at current energy prices
options.feedback: A financial argument in financial language. This is the one that wins budget decisions.

options.text: Two of our three largest clients now ask about this in tenders
options.feedback: Ties sustainability to revenue. Very effective.

options.text: Upcoming reporting requirements will make this mandatory within two years
options.feedback: Reframes a cost as bringing forward an unavoidable one: a strong argument.

options.text: It's the right thing to do for the planet
options.feedback: True, and on its own it loses budget decisions. Use it to frame the case, never as the argument.

options.text: Our competitors are already doing it
options.feedback: Weak on its own. The obvious reply is 'and are they seeing a return?'

options.text: Staff have said they'd feel better about working here
options.feedback: Real but unquantified. It supports a case; it can't carry one.

before.feedback: In a budget meeting, sustainability arguments have to be translated into the language of cost, revenue or risk. The ethical case opens the conversation; the financial case closes it.

after.brief: Same skill: which vocabulary is precise enough for a written business case?
after.prompt: Select every term that carries a specific, checkable meaning.

options.text: carbon footprint
options.feedback: Specific and measurable: total emissions attributable to an activity.

options.text: payback period
options.feedback: Precise financial term: the time for savings to cover the initial cost.

options.text: energy consumption
options.feedback: Directly measurable in kWh.

options.text: waste reduction
options.feedback: Measurable against a baseline.

options.text: eco-friendly
options.feedback: Vague marketing language with no agreed definition. Avoid it in a business case.

options.text: green
options.feedback: Too loose to mean anything specific in a written case.

options.text: sustainable
options.feedback: Useful as a heading, but on its own it commits to nothing measurable.

after.feedback: The test for a business case is whether someone could check the claim in twelve months. 'Carbon footprint' passes; 'eco-friendly' does not.

before.brief: A planning meeting. Sort the sentences by future form.
before.prompt: Put each sentence into the right group.

items.text: I'm meeting the client on Tuesday.
We're having lunch with the team on Friday.
We're going to hire two new people.
She's going to start a new project in May.
OK, I'll call him now.
The printer is broken? I'll use the other one.

before.feedback: Things in your calendar: present continuous. Plans you made before: 'going to'. Decisions you make now: 'will'.

after.brief: Same skill, in a chat with a colleague.

items.text: I'm going to visit the Madrid office next month.
We're going to change the website in June.
Tom is going to lead the new project.
It's cold in here. I'll close the window.
You're busy? No problem, I'll do it.
There's no coffee? I'll buy some.

after.feedback: Use 'going to' for plans you made before. Use 'will' when you decide at the moment of speaking.

before.brief: In a job interview, the interviewer says:
before.message: Tell me about your last project.
before.prompt: Which answer is best?

options.text: Last year I worked on our new website. I planned the pages, and we finished in May.
options.feedback: Good. Past simple for a finished project, and you say what you did.

options.text: Last year I have worked on our new website.
options.feedback: With 'last year', use the past simple: 'I worked'.

options.text: I work on our new website last year.
options.feedback: 'Last year' is in the past. Use 'worked', not 'work'.

options.text: It was a very interesting project.
options.feedback: Correct, but you don't say what you did.

after.brief: Next question:
after.message: What are you doing in your job at the moment?

options.text: I'm working on a new app for our customers. I design the screens.
options.feedback: Correct. Present continuous for work happening now, and present simple for your usual job.

options.text: I worked on a new app at the moment.
options.feedback: 'At the moment' means now. Don't use the past simple.

options.text: I'm work on a new app.
options.feedback: Add -ing: 'I'm working'.

options.text: I have a job in a big company.
options.feedback: Correct, but it doesn't say what you are doing now.

before.brief: A colleague messages you: 'Can you look at the Vidal deck before 2?'  You can, but not until 1:30.
before.prompt: Which reply is best for chat?

options.text: Yes — I'll get to it around 1:30, so you'll have comments before 2. 👍
options.feedback: Answers the question, gives the actual time, and confirms the deadline is safe. Everything they need in one line.

options.text: Yes
options.feedback: Answers but leaves them wondering when, so they may chase you at 1:45.

options.text: I'm quite busy this morning but I should be able to fit it in at some point, I'll try my best to get to it before your deadline if nothing else comes up.
options.feedback: Far too long for chat, and after all those words they still don't know if they'll have it.

options.text: Sure thing!! No problem at all!! 😄😄
options.feedback: Friendly but no time given, and the punctuation is doing a lot of work for a routine request.

after.brief: Different ping: 'Quick one — do we have budget for the extra shoot?' You do not know.

options.text: Not sure — Elena owns that budget line. I'll ask her now and come back to you within the hour.
options.feedback: Says you don't know, names who does, and commits to a time. This is the most useful 'I don't know' you can send.

options.text: I don't know.
options.feedback: True, and it leaves them exactly where they started.

options.text: I think so? Probably fine.
options.feedback: Guessing about money. If it's wrong, someone books a shoot that isn't funded.

options.text: Let me check and I'll let you know.
options.feedback: Helpful. It just doesn't say when, so they don't know whether to wait or chase.

before.brief: You are writing your daily update in the team chat.
before.message: Yesterday I ______ the new login page.
before.prompt: Which word is correct?

options.text: finished
options.feedback: Correct. 'Yesterday' needs the past simple: 'finished'.

options.text: finish
options.feedback: 'Yesterday' is in the past. Use 'finished'.

options.text: am finishing
options.feedback: The present continuous is for now, not for yesterday.

options.text: have finished
options.feedback: Close, but don't use 'have finished' with 'yesterday'.

after.brief: A different chat. Your manager asks where you are today. You reply:
after.message: Sorry, I ______ from home today. My train is cancelled.

options.text: 'm working
options.feedback: Correct. The present continuous is for what is happening now or today.

options.text: worked
options.feedback: That's the past. 'Today' needs 'I'm working'.

options.text: work
options.feedback: The present simple is for habits, like 'I work from home on Fridays'.

options.text: 'm work
options.feedback: Add -ing: 'I'm working'.

before.brief: A customer comes to your desk. He is angry.
before.message: I ordered this two weeks ago, and it still hasn't arrived!
before.prompt: What do you say first?

options.text: I'm sorry about that. Let me check your order now.
options.feedback: Good. Say sorry, then do something.

options.text: Calm down, please.
options.feedback: This makes angry people angrier.

options.text: It's not my fault.
options.feedback: Maybe true, but the customer needs help, not an excuse.

options.text: Sorry.
options.feedback: Polite, but what happens next? Offer to help.

after.brief: A different customer calls. Yesterday you gave her the wrong price.

options.text: I'm sorry, I gave you the wrong price. The correct price is €40. I'll email it to you now.
options.feedback: Good. A short apology, the correct information, and what you will do.

options.text: I apologise you for the price.
options.feedback: Grammar mistake. Say 'I apologise for the mistake', with no person after 'apologise'.

options.text: The price on the website was wrong, not me.
options.feedback: Don't blame. Say sorry and give the correct price.

options.text: Oh, sorry! My mistake! I'm so sorry! Really sorry!
options.feedback: Too many apologies. Say sorry once, then give the correct price.

before.brief: You are starting a short presentation for a client. Put your opening in order.
before.prompt: Put the lines in the best order.
items: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for coming.
My name is Ana, and I work in the design team.
Today I'm going to show you our new logo.
First, I'm going to explain the idea. Then I'll show you three designs.
At the end, you can ask questions.
before.feedback: Hello and thanks, who you are, the topic, the plan, then questions. 'Going to' tells people your plan.

after.brief: Same skill, at the end of a different presentation, for your own team.
after.prompt: Put the lines in the best order.
items: OK, that's the end of my presentation.
The main point is: we're going to open the new shop in June.
I'm going to send you the full plan next week.
Thank you for listening.
Are there any questions?
after.feedback: Say it's the end and repeat the main point. Then give the next step, say thank you, and ask for questions.

before.brief: A colleague asks you a question over coffee.
before.prompt: Do you prefer working at home or in the office? Why?
checklist: I said my opinion clearly (I think… / In my opinion…)
I gave at least one reason with 'because'
I gave a small example from my work
I spoke for about 30 seconds
before.model: In my opinion, working in the office is better for me. I think it's easier to ask questions, because my colleagues are next to me. For example, last week I had a problem with a report, and my manager helped me in five minutes. But I like working at home on Fridays, because it's quiet.
before.feedback: Opinion, reason, example. This simple plan works for almost any question.

after.brief: A different question, in a team meeting.
after.prompt: What is the best day of the week for team meetings? Why?
checklist: I gave a clear answer (I think… / In my opinion…)
I gave a reason with 'because'
I said one problem with a different day
I finished with a short summary (So, I think…)
after.model: I think Tuesday is the best day for team meetings. On Monday, everyone is busy with emails from the weekend. On Friday, some people work from home. Tuesday is good because we have time to plan the week. So, I think Tuesday morning is best.
after.feedback: A clear opinion, a reason, and a short summary at the end. That is enough for a strong answer.

before.brief: A job interview. The interviewer asks: 'Tell me about your job.'
before.message: I work in the finance ______. I'm responsible for the invoices.
before.prompt: Which word is correct?

options.text: department
options.feedback: Correct. A department is a part of a company, like Finance or Sales.

options.text: responsible
options.feedback: 'Responsible' is an adjective: 'I'm responsible for…'. It is not a place.

options.text: colleague
options.feedback: A colleague is a person, not a part of a company.

options.text: office
options.feedback: Possible, but 'the finance department' is the usual phrase.

after.brief: Next question: 'Who do you work with?'
after.message: I work with five ______, and my manager is the head of finance.

options.text: colleagues
options.feedback: Correct. Colleagues are the people you work with.

options.text: companions
options.feedback: A false friend. At work, say 'colleagues', not 'companions'.

options.text: clients
options.feedback: Clients buy from your company. They are not in your team.

options.text: bosses
options.feedback: Informal, and you have one manager, not five bosses.

before.brief: Your colleague Marta is sick today. You answer her phone. A client says his name very fast.
before.prompt: What do you say?

options.text: Sorry, could you spell your name, please?
options.feedback: Good. Now you can write the name correctly.

options.text: What is your name? Say it again.
options.feedback: Clear, but it sounds like an order. Add 'sorry' and 'could you'.

options.text: OK, thank you.
options.feedback: You didn't understand the name. Now you can't help him.

options.text: Can you spell me your name?
options.feedback: Say 'Could you spell your name, please?' Don't put 'me' after 'spell'.

after.brief: A different call. Marta's manager asks you to do something. There are two files: the price list and the contract.
after.message: Can you send the file to the client today?
after.prompt: You don't know which file. What do you say?

options.text: Sure. Do you mean the price list or the contract?
options.feedback: Good. Two choices make the question quick to answer.

options.text: Which file? I don't understand.
options.feedback: OK, but give two choices. It's faster.

options.text: Sure, no problem.
options.feedback: You don't know which file. You may send the wrong one.

options.text: Can you explain me which file?
options.feedback: Say 'explain to me', or just ask 'Which file do you mean?'

before.brief: You need the meeting link from a colleague. You write in the team chat.
before.prompt: Which message is best for chat?

options.text: Hi Sam, could you send me the link for the 3 p.m. meeting, please?
options.feedback: Friendly, polite and clear. Perfect for chat.

options.text: Link.
options.feedback: Too short. It sounds like an order.

options.text: Dear Mr Jones, I would be very grateful if you could kindly send me the link.
options.feedback: Much too formal for a chat with a colleague.

options.text: Hi Sam, are you there?
options.feedback: Friendly, but it doesn't say what you need. Sam has to ask.
